facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The Archaeological Survey of India has declared the temple an ancient and historical monument under Act No. LXXI of 1951, dt.28/11/1951.
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India declared the circular Chausath Yogini Temple at Mitaoli a protected monument of national importance under Act LXXI on 28 November 1951.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: According to an inscription dated to 1323 CE (Vikram Samvat 1383), the temple was built by the Kachchhapaghata king Devapala (r. c. 1055 – 1075).
facts.text: An inscription discovered on a slab in the temple dates to the year 1323 CE, recording patronage under King Devapala of the Kachchhapaghata dynasty.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The temple is formed by a circular wall with 65 chambers, apparently for 64 yoginis and the goddess Devi, and an open mandapa in the centre of a circular courtyard, sacred to Shiva.
facts.text: The hilltop temple is constructed with an outer circular wall enclosing 65 small chambers arranged around an open courtyard with a central circular shrine dedicated to Shiva.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The temple is located on a hill about 100 feet (30 m) in height; there are 100 steps to climb up to the entrance.
facts.text: The temple complex stands on an isolated hill rising approximately 30 metres in height and is reached by a flight of 100 steps.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Within the main central shrine there are slab coverings which have perforations in them to drain rainwater to a large underground storage.
facts.text: The central Shiva shrine incorporates an ancient drainage system with perforated roof slabs designed to channel rainwater into an underground storage facility.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The first mention of the place and its inscriptions was in the Gwalior State Archaeological Department's report of 1915-16.
facts.text: Archaeological officer M. B. Garde first formally surveyed and reported the Mitawali temple and its inscriptions in the 1915–16 annual report of the Gwalior State Archaeological Department.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: As no foundation inscription has been found and therefore dating of the temple is a matter of contention among scholars.
facts.text: Historians disagree whether the inscription dated to 1323 CE records the original construction of the temple or a 14th-century renovation of a pre-existing 11th-century structure by the Kachchhapaghatas.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: It is said that the temple was the venue of providing education in astrology and mathematics based on the transit of the Sun.
facts.text: Regional folklore maintains that the circular temple operated as an esoteric academy where students and practitioners were instructed in mathematics and astrology based on the movement of the sun.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: This is because they were designed for communion with yoginis, thought to be capable of flight.
facts.text: Local tradition recounts that the circular courtyard was deliberately left roofless so that the 64 yoginis could alight from flight to partake in nocturnal tantric rituals.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: The Agni Purana (chapters 52 and 146) lists the names of 64 yoginis and their ritual invocations around Bhairava.
facts.text: Tantric chapters in the Agni Purana enumerate sixty-four yoginis around Shiva and outline circular mandala arrangements for their esoteric worship.
